But sometimes, when you’re wrong, you’re really wrong. Wake Forest went on to win 49-7. So much for that prolific SMU offense.

articles.title: At least 100 people pulled from Mississippi River after New Orleans ship crash as lengthy salvage effort looms
articles.summary: Officials say roughly 100 people were pulled from the Mississippi River after the Atlantic Asphalt tanker struck the docked American Heritage cruise ship in New Orleans on Friday.
articles.body: Roughly 100 people were pulled from the Mississippi River after a tanker struck a docked cruise ship in New Orleans on Friday, officials revealed Saturday, as the U.S. Coast Guard prepares for a potentially weeks-long operation to remove the capsized vessel. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said 191 passengers and crew members were aboard the American Heritage when the Atlantic Asphalt tanker struck the vessel near the Port of New Orleans. Everyone survived, though eight people remained hospitalized Saturday, including two in serious condition. The other six patients were stable, officials said. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said crews were preparing to remove 16,000 gallons of fuel from the American Heritage before salvage operations begin. Divers were expected to assess the vessel, while pollution response teams monitored the river for potential leaks. NEW ORLEANS BOAT CRASH CALLED ‘MIRACLE ON THE MISSISSIPPI’ AS EVERYONE IS ACCOUNTED FOR, OFFICIALS SAY Burnham said crews had not observed any product in the river requiring removal but warned that hazardous materials could potentially escape during the operation. "As the mayor said, we're talking weeks, we're not talking days, we're talking weeks. So we're going to do this safely, and we're going to make sure that it's done right," Burnham said. Moreno also revealed that the American Heritage's captain was injured but remained aboard until passengers and crew were accounted for, becoming the last person to leave the vessel. "Every moment of the critical time [Friday], he did not want to leave his ship," Moreno said. TWO DEAD, INCLUDING INFANT, AFTER BOAT CAPSIZES IN NEW YORK HARBOR; 12 RESCUED The captain initially refused medical treatment until he knew where everyone was, according to the mayor. Port of New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montro said responders evacuated more than 80 people before the vessel overturned, while roughly 100 people ended up in the river. Montro said she estimated the American Heritage capsized within 30 to 45 minutes of the collision, though the exact timeline remains under investigation. Officials credited life jackets and the rapid response of emergency crews and nearby vessels with preventing fatalities. Investigators are examining a possible steering issue involving the tanker, though the exact cause of the collision remains unknown. "I can say though I do not have any indication that this is terrorism related in any way, shape or form, but again, the investigators will continue to keep working through that," Burnham said. 11-NIGHT CARIBBEAN CRUISE ABRUPTLY CANCELED AFTER COAST GUARD DETAINS SHIP The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) confirmed Saturday that investigators recovered the Atlantic Asphalt's voyage data recorder, which captures information including the vessel's speed, course and audio from its bridge. NTSB board member John DeLeeuw said during a news conference Saturday that investigators will also examine the tanker's maintenance records and mechanical history as they work to determine what caused the collision. He cautioned that the agency remains in the early stages of gathering evidence and has not reached any conclusions. DeLeeuw and a team of NTSB investigators began arriving Saturday after travel disruptions delayed its response. DeLeeuw said 16 investigators were on scene and preparing to interview crew members and others involved. The agency said it expects to release a preliminary report in about 30 days, with a final report identifying probable causes and potential safety recommendations expected in 18 to 24 months. The collision occurred around 12:30 p.m. local time Friday, when the tanker struck the American Heritage, which had been docked for approximately two hours. The vessel began taking on water before capsizing. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Atlantic Asphalt has since been moved from the collision site, while the Coast Guard has partially reopened the river to two-way traffic. A 500-foot safety zone remains in place around the wreck. American Cruise Lines, which operates American Heritage, is coordinating with local officials to assist displaced passengers as the investigation and recovery efforts continue.

articles.body: In December 1976, a seven-year-old boy named Craig wrote to Santa Claus after no presents had arrived the previous Christmas, and he drew a map to his home in case Santa had got lost. The letter never reached the North Pole. It arrived at Francisco’s, a restaurant in Seattle, where owner Dick Francisco read it and founded The Forgotten Children’s Fund that night. That first Christmas reached 285 children in 81 families. According to the Fund’s website, the all-volunteer charity has since served more than 19,000 families and hand-delivered more than 400,000 gifts, and it marks its fiftieth Christmas in 2026.What happened to Craig's letter to Santa in December 1976According to the Fund's home page, the story began with a letter from seven-year-old Craig, who feared that Santa had got lost the year before, when no presents arrived. Craig drew Santa a map to his home. The page states that a group of Seattle friends read the letter and made a promise that no child in their corner of the world should ever wonder whether Santa had forgotten them. The home page adds that, fifty years later, "Santa has never once needed the map."The 50 Years page gives the setting in more detail. According to that page, Craig's letter was written in December 1976 and never reached the North Pole. It reached Francisco's, a restaurant in Seattle, and immediately captured the heart of Dick Francisco. The page says The Forgotten Children's Fund was created that night to help others in similar situations. A caption on the page shares part of the letter itself, in which Craig wrote: "Moma said you got lost last year… so here is a map."How did the charity deliver its first Christmas gifts to 285 children in 81 familiesThe 50 Years page profiles the Fund's founder as Richard "Buck" Francisco, whom it describes as a Marine and restaurateur. According to the page, Francisco read Craig's letter at his restaurant one December night and decided on the spot that Santa would never miss another house in Seattle. The page states that he spent the rest of his life keeping that promise. It also records that Dick Francisco passed away in 2016 at the age of 92, and that every doorbell rung at Christmas since then rings in his honour.The first Christmas was a much smaller operation than the one the Fund runs today. Both pages of the Fund's website state that it reached 285 children in 81 families that year. According to the 50 Years timeline, routes pushed beyond King County in the 1980s, and volunteer Santas and elf crews became the heart of the operation. The page adds that the ranch owners also began serving children beyond Christmas during that decade.Charity identifies children who need the most support during ChristmasAccording to the Fund's home page, every dollar comes from individuals and partner businesses; there are no paid staff, and donations become gifts rather than overhead. The page explains that the process starts when a parent applies. Volunteers then call the family and listen for the one thing each child is hoping Santa remembers. The page states that applications open in the autumn and close in mid-December, and that each application is screened with care so that limited resources reach the children with the greatest need.The home page says volunteers hand-wrap more than 22,000 gifts, each chosen for one specific child. It describes the delivery as Santa sitting down with the family, staying while the children open a present, and leaving the rest under the tree with warm blankets and Christmas dinner. According to the 50 Years page, the work is based each season in a donated warehouse of up to 50,000 square feet, which is turned into a wrap centre. The same page records that in 2017 a hot real-estate market left the Fund without a warehouse, and that a building slated for demolition became that season's North Pole after news coverage brought dozens of leads.How many children and families did the charity reach across Washington in 2025The 50 Years page states that in 2025 more than 3,500 volunteers wrapped more than 22,000 gifts and assembled hundreds of new bikes. It reports that this reached 2,100 children and 750 families across eight Washington counties. The page sets the 285 children of 1976 beside the 2,100-plus children of 2026. The home page lists the Fund's overall figures as more than 19,000 families served, more than 400,000 gifts hand-delivered, more than 3,500 volunteers each season, and 100% volunteers.The Fund also runs a programme outside December. According to the home page, the M-Bar-C Ranch on Whidbey Island hosts a Day of Western Fun for groups of children and adults with special needs. The 50 Years page describes it as a 60-acre ranch that became the Fund's year-round programme in the 1990s, and says it now serves 2,500 children a year. It adds that Dick Francisco, Don Rall and other families had bought the ranch for their own children and then repurposed it for the Fund. The timeline ends with the fiftieth Christmas in 2026, fifty years after one letter went to the wrong address.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Born in England in 1945, Rod Anderson spent 81 years not knowing his father was a Canadian soldier; after an 18-year family search, a DNA match connected him with a 77-year-old half-sister in Ontario
articles.summary: For 81 years, Rod Anderson had one question that he could never quit find an answer to: who was his father?
articles.body: For 81 years, Rod Anderson had one question that he could never quit find an answer to: who was his father? Born in Farnham, England, in 1945, Anderson grew up with his British mother, Yvonne, without knowing much about the man whose DNA he shared. He spent nearly 50 years trying to identify him, even taking a DNA test to investigate someone he suspected could be his biological father. The results, however, ruled that person out.Little did he know that thousands of miles away, a Canadian family was trying to solve the same mystery. An 18-year search, a handful of old family documents and an unexpected DNA match would eventually bring the two sides together, revealing that Anderson's father had been a Canadian soldier stationed in Britain during the Second World War.A family rumour that refused to disappearThe story began with Charles Blakney, a Canadian soldier from New Brunswick. Before leaving for England, Blakney was married and had a baby daughter back home. In 1942, he boarded the HMT Andes to serve overseas, eventually working as a motor and driver mechanic with the New Brunswick Rangers.But there was a family rumour that followed him home. Blakney had apparently fathered a child with a woman in England.His granddaughter, Bethany Allen, had heard different versions of the story growing up. Some members of the family knew about it, while others had never heard a word. Determined to establish whether there was any truth to it, Allen requested her grandfather's divorce records from the archives in 2008. The documents confirmed that a child had indeed been born in England during the war.There was just one problem. The records established that the baby existed, but they did not reveal his identity or what had happened to him. Allen's mother, who was Blakney's daughter, had always wanted to find her missing sibling. Before she died, she asked Allen to keep searching and find out whether he had grown up happy and healthy.For almost two decades, the search continued without a name or face to attach to the mystery. Then, in spring 2026, Allen took an Ancestry DNA test. The results pointed to an unexpected match: Rodney Anderson, living in Surrey, England. He was her half-uncle.Allen managed to locate Anderson's daughter, Dawn Roberts, the same day. Roberts called her father with the news that a woman in Canada was looking for him. Anderson initially thought it was a prank. Instead, he had finally found the answer he had spent decades looking for.When war brought people togetherAnderson's story belongs to a much larger chapter of the Second World War, one shaped by the movement of soldiers across borders and the relationships they formed along the way.Although Britain and Canada shared close historical and political ties, Canada entered the Second World War independently, declaring war on Germany on September 10, 1939, a week after Britain. As part of the Allied war effort, hundreds of thousands of Canadian servicemen were stationed in Britain, which became an important base for training, military preparations and the campaigns to liberate occupied Europe.For young men living far from home, everyday life was not limited to military duties. They interacted with local communities, attended social gatherings and formed relationships with British women. Some of these relationships resulted in marriages and families that would eventually cross the Atlantic.The scale of this movement was considerable. Between 1942 and 1948, around 48,000 war brides, accompanied by approximately 22,000 children, travelled to Canada, most of them from Britain. Halifax's Pier 21 became an important arrival point for these women and their families.But the story of wartime relationships was not limited to marriages. Canadian military records documented tens of thousands of overseas marriages and the children born within them. Yet these figures did not account for unclaimed war births. The official movement of wives and children to Canada was organised around recognised marriages, leaving other family situations outside the same system.The family secrets left behind by warHaving a child outside marriage in 1940s Britain could carry considerable social stigma. Women often faced disproportionate blame and judgement, while the fathers could return to their home countries and leave the mothers to navigate the consequences.Historian Jeff Noakes of the Canadian War Museum told CBC News that there was considerable shame attached to these pregnancies, and that the blame fell disproportionately on women. Some children were placed for adoption, while others grew up with their parentage concealed or never fully explained.It is important, however, not to assume that every family had the same experience. We do not know precisely why Anderson's mother never discussed his father, or what Blakney knew about his son. What we do know is that the social climate made such family histories particularly difficult to talk about.The issue was not confined to Britain either. Canadian soldiers also formed relationships with women in countries such as the Netherlands, which Canadian forces helped liberate in 1945. Their presence sometimes caused friction with local communities. Dutch newspapers even published criticism of the soldiers' influence on local morality, prompting Canadian military commander Lieutenant-General Guy Simonds to defend his troops publicly.A resemblance across generationsToday, Anderson has a 77-year-old half-sister, Barb Lowe, living in St. Thomas, Ontario. The two speak every week and say they felt an immediate connection when they first spoke. Lowe has noticed similarities between Anderson and their father, who died in 1987. At one point, she even pointed out that they had the same ears.There was another unexpected resemblance. Anderson lost an arm and an eye in a railway accident as a child. Despite being told in a government assessment that he would be unable to work as a mechanic, he eventually trained in the trade and opened his own business. It turned out that his biological father had also been a motor mechanic.For Anderson, learning about his father has meant discovering something about himself, too. He now has relatives in Canada, a family history he can finally trace and connections that will extend to his children and grandchildren.There may still be another mystery to solve. The divorce documents that helped Allen identify Anderson also referred to another baby Blakney had fathered in Britain during the war. The family is now looking into whether that child, too, might be somewhere waiting to be found.More than 8 decades after the end of the war, its consequences are still unfolding in unexpected ways. For some families, the conflict meant separation, migration and years of unanswered questions. For Anderson, a DNA match has finally given a name to the man he spent most of his life searching for, and brought him a family he never knew he had.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Costco-brand whipped cream recalled over potential presence of cleaning chemical
articles.summary: Costco members who love a whipped topping may consider going à la mode with their favorite dessert instead after the retailer’s Kirkland-brand whipped cream was recalled.
articles.body: Costco members who love a whipped topping may consider going à la mode with their favorite dessert instead after the retailer’s Kirkland-brand whipped cream was recalled. Cans of Kirkland Signature Real Heavy Whipped Cream sold between Oct. 11 and Oct. 31 are subject to a voluntary recall after some customers reported a chemical taste and smell. Alamance Foods, the manufacturer, said it has received no reports of serious effects requiring medical care. “We have learned that one batch of Kirkland Signature Whipped Cream may contain a small amount of a cleaning chemical,” the company said. The product was sold in Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee and Wisconsin. Customers can return the cream to Costco for a full refund, according to Alamance Foods.

articles.title: National Library of Wales exhibit brings Kyffin Williams' work 'to life'
articles.summary: Technology similar to that used for exhibitions of Van Gogh, Cézanne and LS Lowry is being used.
articles.body:
For the first time, the paintings of Sir Kyffin Williams have been brought to life in a new immersive experience at the National Library of Wales.

Technology similar to that used for exhibitions of Van Gogh, Cézanne and LS Lowry will immerse visitors in the mountain landscapes, hillfarms and stormy seas created by the painter, who is considered the defining Welsh artist of the 20th Century.

Images from Williams's oil paintings such as the hill farmer and sheepdog are animated in a 360-degree centrepiece and Sir Kyffin's life story is narrated by Sir Bryn Terfel in a bilingual presentation, with original paintings illuminated on the walls.

The National Library, which received grants of £500,000 to fund the project, said it hoped it will introduce a new audience to Sir Kyffin's work.

There are also interactive installations including a recreation of a self-portrait which can be touched, giving visitors a sense of the texture of Sir Kyffin's oil paintings.

He painted using an impasto technique - where paint is applied so thickly on to a canvas that it stands out in three dimensions.

Sir Kyffin, who was born on Anglesey in 1918, had a long relationship with the National Library, in Aberystwyth, Ceredigion, which has about 2,000 pieces of his work in its collection.

In 1950 the library bought its first two pieces from the young artist soon after he left the Slade School of Fine Art in London.

Morfudd Bevan, art curator at the National Library of Wales, said the library paid £15 for an oil painting of Cader Idris and £7.10 for an ink and wash drawing of Tre'r Ceiri on the Llŷn Peninsula.

Today, original work by Sir Kyffin sells for tens of thousands of pounds.

Bevan added: "The library saw the potential of this young artist.

"It was really important that we were encouraging and supporting young artists at the beginning of their careers, when Kyffin was trying to establish himself as a professional artist."

It was the start of a close bond with the artist.

When he died in September 2006, he left a substantial part of his estate to the library, more than 1,200 works on paper, about 200 oil paintings, more than 300 original prints and his personal archive.

The national library holds the largest collection of Sir Kyffin's work in the world.

The library hopes the new attraction will introduce more people to his work.

Director of experience Carys Ifan said: "It's by no means a traditional exhibition.

"You go on a journey, literally moving through three rooms that used to be old offices. They've been repurposed because we are so keen to open up more and more to the public."

Profiad Kyffin Experience was made possible by technology invented by Focal Studios, an immersive experience company and the main designers of the exhibition.

Chief executive Dennis Outten said working on the project had been a "labour of love" and an "incredible journey for everyone involved".

Focal Studios worked with another company, leo&hyde, to animate Sir Kyffin's paintings in a 360-degree immersive experience so they come alive in projections on the walls and floor.

"It's like you're in one of his paintings, I love it," Outten said.

"It's not like virtual reality, because you can hold the hand of your child, you can sit there with your grandmother or your friend and you experience it together. I think that's incredibly powerful."

Inside the "projection cave", visitors see scenes painted by Sir Kyffin come alive as the cattle, waterfalls, the farmer and his sheepdog move around them.

Outten said high fidelity scans of Sir Kyffin's original work and creative techniques helped bring the paintings to life.

"We actually created a 3D model of Kyffin's farmer and dog, and then using animation techniques, puppeteering them essentially to move."

Rhodri Llwyd Morgan, the library's chief executive, said the new experience is part of a strategy "to be more popular, more appealing and that's our aim".

The experience was formally launched on Thursday and opens to the public from 18 November.

articles.title: A Texas woman fought the court-ordered sale of her marital home after a receiver received a $685,000 offer; despite a divorce decree awarding her 60% of net proceeds, an appeals court upheld the sale and related orders
articles.summary: A Texas woman challenged a court-ordered sale of the home she once shared with her former husband after a receiver received an offer of $685,000,
articles.body: A Texas woman challenged a court-ordered sale of the home she once shared with her former husband after a receiver received an offer of $685,000, according to the Justia U.S. Law case record for the Second Court of Appeals at Fort Worth. Although her divorce decree awarded her 60 percent of the net proceeds from the sale, the appellate court upheld the lower court’s decision to allow the receiver to proceed and affirmed the related orders.The dispute illustrates how limited a former spouse’s control can be after a divorce court orders a marital residence sold. Even where a decree spells out how the money will be divided, a receiver may still be empowered to market, contract for, and complete the sale when the parties cannot or will not carry out the court’s instructions themselves.What the decree providedThe case arose after a Texas divorce court entered a decree dividing the couple’s marital property. Under the decree, the woman was to receive 60 percent of the net proceeds generated by the sale of the marital home, while the remaining share belonged to her former husband.That allocation gave her a significant financial stake in the outcome of the transaction.But that didn’t necessarily give her unilateral power to refuse an offer, stall the closing or stop the property from being sold if the court had already decided that a receiver should be running the process.The receiver was later presented with an offer to buy the home for $685,000.The woman objected to the sale and asked the court to intervene, saying the deal should not go ahead against her wishes.Why a receiver was involvedA receiver is a neutral person appointed by a court to take control of specific property or carry out a particular task. In divorce cases, receivers are sometimes appointed to sell a home when former spouses cannot agree on listing terms, refuse to cooperate, or otherwise make it difficult to enforce the court’s property division.Texas courts have broad discretion to appoint receivers, but the remedy is generally treated as an extraordinary one. In earlier Texas cases, appellate courts have emphasised that a receiver may be used when a marital residence cannot practically be divided between the parties and a sale is necessary to effect a just and right division of the community estate.In this matter, the trial court had already put the sale process in motion through the receiver. The woman’s challenge therefore focused not simply on whether she wanted the house sold, but on whether the court could allow the receiver to accept and proceed with the $685,000 offer despite her objections.The woman’s objectionsThe woman argued that the court should not permit the sale because she held a 60 percent interest in the net proceeds under the divorce decree. From her perspective, allowing the receiver to complete the transaction without her agreement risked undermining the property division the court had previously ordered.She also challenged the receiver’s authority and the related orders connected to the sale. Her position was that the receiver should not be able to take an offer, negotiate the terms, or close the sale while she remained opposed to the transaction.Those concerns are understandable in practical terms. A marital home is often a family’s most valuable asset, and the difference between an acceptable sale price and an unacceptable one can amount to tens of thousands of dollars, particularly after closing costs, commissions, mortgage payoffs, and other deductions are considered.What the appeals court decidedThe Second Court of Appeals at Fort Worth rejected the woman’s challenge. The court affirmed the trial court’s orders, including the authorization for the receiver to proceed with the sale of the marital residence.In doing so, the appellate court effectively held that the woman’s 60 percent share of the net proceeds did not give her the power to block the receiver’s court-authorised sale. The decree determined how the proceeds would be divided after the sale, but it did not convert her interest into a veto over the receiver’s authority to sell the property.The court also upheld the related orders challenged in the appeal. That meant the receiver could continue performing the duties assigned by the trial court, including pursuing the $685,000 offer and carrying out the sale process.Why the ruling mattersThe decision is important because it clarifies the difference between an ownership interest in sale proceeds and control over the sale itself. A divorce decree can award a spouse a percentage of the net proceeds, but that financial entitlement does not automatically give that spouse the right to stop a court-supervised transaction.For homeowners facing a similar situation, the ruling underscores the need to act early. Objections to a receiver’s appointment, the proposed listing strategy, or the terms of a sale generally need to be raised promptly in the trial court, where the judge can consider the evidence and decide whether the receiver’s actions are consistent with the divorce decree.It also highlights the value of clear language in divorce decrees. A decree that says a spouse will receive a percentage of net proceeds is different from one that gives that spouse approval rights over offers, listing prices, closing dates, or the selection of a buyer. The more specific the decree, the easier it is for both parties and the receiver to understand who may make which decisions.The broader lessonDivorce cases involving real estate often become difficult because the home represents both money and memory. One former spouse may see a sale as a necessary step toward closure, while the other may see it as the loss of a home, a neighbourhood, or a financial safety net.Courts must balance those human concerns against the need to enforce their orders. When parties cannot agree, a receiver can provide a way to move the process forward without leaving the property idle, allowing debt to accumulate, or permitting one spouse to prevent the other from receiving an ordered share of the proceeds.In this Texas case, the woman’s 60 percent share remained protected in principle. What the appeals court made clear was that her share did not give her the final word on whether the home would be sold. The receiver’s $685,000 offer could proceed, and the related orders authorising that process would stand.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: New Orleans port sues tanker owners over cruise ship collision for $1m
articles.summary: The lawsuit filed by New Orleans officials also requests that the tanker involved in the collision with the cruise ship be seized and sold to pay for damages.
articles.body:
The Port of New Orleans is suing the owners and managers of a tanker that crashed into a cruise ship docked in New Orleans on Friday.

The port is claiming the tanker is at fault for the collision that saw more than 100 passengers being rescued from the Mississippi River and caused more than $1m (£756k) in damage, according to court documents.

The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one was unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi".

The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Capt Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering."

The paddlewheel cruise ship, American Heritage, was left on its side and partially submerged in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel Atlantic Asphalt on Friday afternoon.

The court documents added that the port terminal "was significantly damaged" in the incident.

The tanker, the M/V Atlantic Asphalt, its owner Nave Shipping SA, and its management company, Thome Ship Management Pte Ltd, are all named in the federal court lawsuit filed on Friday in the Eastern District of Louisiana court.

Officials are still investigating the full extent of the damage from the crash, as well as the cause, but the lawsuit says the port is looking for money to cover cleanup, inspections, repairs and other expenses.

The lawsuit requests that the tanker be seized and sold to pay for the damage. It also alleges that the collision "occurred as a result of the negligence, gross negligence, fault or carelessness" of the ship and operating companies.

It alleges that the tanker and companies failed "to use all available means to avoid the risk" of colliding with the riverboat.

Nave Shipping is a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation. BBC has contacted the China State Shipbuilding Corporation for comment.

Thome Ship Management has also been contacted. The firm said in a statement on Saturday that the crew of the Atlantic Asphalt were safe and accounted for.

"OSM Thome is fully complying with the local authorities as they carry out the necessary investigations," it said.

There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the port authority.

Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help while officials shut down traffic in the Mississippi River during the rescue effort.

The American Heritage had been finishing an eight-day cruise calling at destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi along the waterway.

articles.title: Explosion near Syria’s capital kills father and child
articles.summary: Syria’s Internal Security Forces have launched an investigation into a suspected bomb attack in a suburb of Damascus.
articles.body:
A blast from a suspected explosive device planted inside a car in a suburb of the Syrian capital, Damascus, has killed at least two people, including a child, and wounded one.

The explosion in Jaramana, on the southeastern edge of Damascus, on Saturday killed a man and his daughter, while a third person, said to be the wife of the man, was seriously injured.

Syria’s Internal Security Forces said they sealed off the area and opened an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the blast.

Jaramana is home to a large community of the Druze religious minority and has seen tensions between some Druze members and the Sunni majority backing President Ahmed al-Sharaa’s government.

Witnesses described the vehicle as a Kia Rio parked between two apartment buildings in Jaramana, which is largely considered a quiet residential area, said Al Jazeera’s Heidi Pett, reporting from the blast scene.

Pett said the security situation in the capital remains complex, despite improvements since the regime of former President Bashar al-Assad fell two years ago.

“In the last couple of months, there were two very high-profile incidents,” she said, including a double-tap attack in July during French President Emmanuel Macron’s visit, which Syrian authorities attributed to a cell affiliated with ISIL (ISIS).

“There was also a deadly attack on what’s known as the Lawyer’s Cafe, near the Palace of Justice, which has been the scene of these high-profile trials of former members of the Assad regime,” Pett said.

She added that most of the bombings and security incidents have not necessarily targeted civilians but members and locations of security forces, which authorities have also blamed on ISIL.

Last year, Damascus joined the US-led international coalition against ISIL. The coalition was formed in 2014 and has carried out operations against the group in Syria and Iraq.

On September 27, the security forces said they had arrested four members of an ISIL cell involved in planning and carrying out several attacks in different parts of the country.

Last month, Syria’s security forces said they foiled a plot to target a police patrol in the Damascus countryside, saying an ISIL cell was preparing to carry out the attack, Syrian state television reported.

They said the group was responsible for explosions and assassinations in Raqqa, Aleppo, Idlib and Homs.

articles.title: Netanyahu says only a unity government can guarantee Israel’s security
articles.summary: Eisenkot, in charge of forming a government, dismisses the appeal as ‘tricks’ as talks and a Knesset speaker vote loom.
articles.body:
Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has renewed his call for a national unity government with his rival, Gadi Eisenkot, saying only such a government can guarantee Israel’s security.

In a video statement on Saturday, Netanyahu said a meeting with Eisenkot on Thursday “only strengthened the conviction that it is essential to form a national unity government”.

The prime minister said such a government could “eliminate the Iranian threat once and for all”, claiming Tehran would “not hesitate to use nuclear weapons against us”.

“Let’s meet in one room, without preconditions,” he said.

Within minutes, however, Eisenkot dismissed the appeal as a ploy.

A former army chief, Eisenkot said Netanyahu “knows he lost the election”.

“Netanyahu is calling for negotiations while they are already underway,” he said. “These tricks don’t work on me.”

Neither side won a majority in the October 27 election. Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc took 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, Eisenkot’s four-party bloc got 48 seats, and Arab-led parties won a record 19.

President Isaac Herzog last week tasked Eisenkot with forming a government, after 67 lawmakers, including those from Arab-led parties, endorsed him, while 46 backed Netanyahu.

Eisenkot has 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension. He has ruled out including Arab-led parties in his government.

Under Eisenkot’s plan for a minority “national emergency government”, his bloc’s 48 lawmakers would vote in favour against the 46 Netanyahu supporters, while the 26 lawmakers from Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties could abstain. It would allow his government to be approved without an absolute majority in the Knesset.

Netanyahu has warned that such a government would lead to Israel’s “collapse”.

Netanyahu’s version would include Jewish parties from the centre and the right and exclude Arab parties . He and his allies have made unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties “stole” the election.

On Friday, Eisenkot called Netanyahu’s campaign against them “racist” .

Eisenkot has said he could work with members of Netanyahu’s Likud party and with Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism if their commitment to unity is “sincere”, but he insisted on a “break with the extremists”, notably supporters of far-right minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.

The Knesset will elect its speaker on Tuesday. The post is currently held by Netanyahu ally Amir Ohana, and the opposition has put forward Matan Kahana, a former military officer, in his place.

articles.title: A 10-year-old Tennessee boy noticed his father's speech slurring as their car swerved on a trip to Georgia; after a crash, Taylor Fritts called 911, helping his dad survive a stroke and earning a hospital certificate
articles.summary: Quick thinking can make all the difference in an emergency; and sometimes, it can even save a life.
articles.body: Quick thinking can make all the difference in an emergency; and sometimes, it can even save a life. When a road trip to Georgia began to steer in the wrong direction, quite literally, 10-year-old Taylor Fritts noticed that something was not right with his father. His speech had started to slur, and the car was swerving dangerously between lanes. What followed was a frightening accident, an emergency call and a decision that would eventually help save his father's life.The fifth grader from Tennessee was travelling to Georgia with his father, Keith Fritts, and his sister in August 2026 when the family encountered an unexpected medical emergency. What was supposed to be an ordinary road trip soon turned into a race against time, as reported by WATE.A road trip takes an unexpected turnThe trouble began somewhere near Sweetwater, Tennessee. Keith had been driving when he suddenly began feeling unwell. His 10-year-old son was among the first to notice that something was different. His father's speech had become unusually slow and slurred, and he appeared increasingly disoriented.Speaking to WATE 6 On Your Side, Keith recalled the moment his son noticed the change. "Somewhere around Sweetwater, things took a turn. And that's when Taylor noticed I was slowing my speech," he said.As Keith's condition worsened, he began struggling to maintain control of the vehicle. The car swerved between lanes, repeatedly veering off the road before returning to it. Taylor recalled how the situation unfolded, describing how they kept drifting off the road and getting back on before eventually crashing into a roadside sign.Even as he experienced a medical emergency, Keith's immediate concern was the safety of his children. Realising that he could no longer control the car properly, he made a deliberate decision to steer it into the sign.Speaking to WATE, he explained that he wanted to ensure that if anyone was injured in the accident, it would be him rather than his children. It was a frightening decision, but one he made with their safety in mind.The collision left the vehicle wrecked. However, Taylor and his sister managed to get out safely. With their father now in need of urgent medical attention, Taylor took the next important step by calling 911.A child's call for help makes all the differenceFollowing Taylor's emergency call, help arrived at the scene. Two truck drivers also stopped along the highway to assist the family while emergency responders attended to Keith.Given the seriousness of his condition, a LIFESTAR medical helicopter was called to transport him to the University of Tennessee Medical Center. Doctors subsequently determined that Keith had suffered a stroke.He spent several days in hospital before recovering and being reunited with his children. Even during the emergency, however, his thoughts had remained with them. Recalling the experience, Keith told WATE that when he was being placed in the ambulance and later the helicopter, he kept asking where his children were.The reunion was an emotional one. Keith recalled having a photograph of himself holding Taylor as a baby, remembering how the nurses had remarked that the little boy was unusually alert and seemed to be looking straight at his father. Years later, that same child had helped save his life.Taylor's actions did not go unnoticed. Following his father's recovery, the hospital recognised him as a 'Stroke Champion' for his bravery and quick thinking. He received a certificate and a gift bag, and was even given the opportunity to sit inside the very LIFESTAR helicopter that had transported his father to hospital.Keith has since spoken warmly about his son's actions, calling him his hero. The two share a close relationship, something Taylor also acknowledged when speaking to WATE. For Keith, however, the experience has only made their bond more meaningful. He said he did not think he could love his son any more than he already did.The family also expressed gratitude towards the two truck drivers who had stopped to help them. They have not yet managed to reconnect with the strangers who offered assistance during those frightening moments.How to recognise a strokeWhile Taylor's actions were remarkable, his father's experience also highlights the importance of recognising the warning signs of a stroke. A stroke occurs when the blood supply to part of the brain is interrupted, either because a blood vessel becomes blocked or because it ruptures. Without an adequate supply of oxygen and nutrients, brain cells begin to suffer damage rapidly.This is why getting medical attention quickly is so important. Brain tissue can begin dying within minutes when it is deprived of oxygen. The sooner doctors can restore blood flow through an obstructed blood vessel, the greater the chances of limiting damage and improving recovery.One way to recognise a possible stroke is through the BE FAST acronym, which helps people remember some of its common warning signs.The letters stand for Balance, Eyes, Face, Arms, Speech and Time. Sudden difficulty maintaining balance, changes in vision, facial drooping, weakness in one arm and slurred or difficult speech can all indicate a stroke. The final letter is a reminder that time is critical. Anyone experiencing these symptoms, or noticing them in someone else, should seek emergency medical assistance immediately.A road trip that began as a family outing became an experience none of them is likely to forget. But amid the wreckage, emergency responders and a frightening medical diagnosis, one thing made all the difference: a young boy with quick thinking and great presence of mind.You use AI every day. articles.title: Tennessee Volunteers overcome sluggish offense, jet lag to take down Texas A&M and keep CFP hopes alive
articles.summary: The Tennessee Volunteers overcame an FAA ground stop delay and a quarterback injury to beat the Texas A&M Aggies on the road to keep CFP hopes alive.
articles.body: Last week, the Tennessee Volunteers needed a fourth quarter explosion to put the Kentucky Wildcats away. History repeated itself seven days later in College Station, as the Vols overcame a sluggish first half and a quarterback injury to vanquish Texas A&M on the road and keep their College Football Playoff hopes alive. Before we go any further, it's important we address the elephant in the room, and that is the FAA ground stop. FAA GROUND STOP LIFTED ON FRIDAY NIGHT, BUT SOME COLLEGE FOOTBALL TEAMS STILL SCRAMBLING TO TRAVEL Although Tennessee coach Josh Heupel likely won't admit it, his team's late arrival in the Lone Star State may have contributed to their sleepy start on offense. The Vols arrived at the team hotel just before 1 a.m. local time, likely offering an explanation for the lack of fireworks on offense. Luckily for Heupel, his defense was up for the challenge, harassing Aggies quarterback Marcel Reed all afternoon to the tune of just 71 yards passing. The Aggies could only muster one touchdown the entire game and were held to only 179 total yards. UPDATED START TIMES FOR COLLEGE FOOTBALL GAMES AFFECTED BY FAA GROUND STOP, BROKEN DOWN BY CONFERENCE It's been a hard fall for Texas A&M, who began the season as a top-10 team before falling out of the AP top-25 entirely. Saturday's loss has the Aggies in danger of missing a bowl game, and they still have a showdown with a surging Texas squad to end the season. For the Vols, a letdown almost surely would have meant the end of their CFP aspirations, as a third loss could have put those dreams on life support. Things looked bleak until, ironically, Tennessee was bit with the injury bug when starting quarterback George MacIntyre went out midway through the third quarter. From that point, the Vols remembered they could run the ball and run it quite well at that, rushing for 196 yards on the day and holding the ball for over 42 minutes. If Tennessee can replicate this formula of salty defense and controlling the time of possession, they will be a hard out in December and beyond. With that in mind, the Vols have a date with the LSU Tigers next Saturday before a road game in Nashville against rival Vanderbilt. If they can navigate that stretch undefeated, they will be a shoo-in to make the CFP. articles.title: The lessons in handshaking and eye contact preparing pupils for the world of work
articles.summary: Year 10 pupils are learning employability skills to reduce the number of young people who end up "Neet".
articles.body:
There is a sudden buzz of conversation in a Year 10 class as teenagers split into pairs, sit down opposite each other and start conducting mock job interviews.

It is not for a forthcoming exam. These 14- and 15-year-olds at Sandbach High School and Sixth Form College are working on skills that should help them when they leave school and try to enter the workforce.

Today, they are learning the art of a successful job interview. Around the room, pupils are practising firm handshakes and making good eye contact.

They are rehearsing how to answer questions that you might expect to be asked in a job interview, such as "When was the last time you worked in a team?" and "Tell me about a time you made a mistake at work".

None of them has even reached working age yet, but in forthcoming lessons they'll also be learning about how to write a CV and what their rights at work are. It is all part of dedicated career lessons that they get every fortnight alongside their usual classes.

There are nearly a million young people across the UK - one in eight of all those aged 16 to 24 - who are not in education, employment or training - or Neet - according to the latest estimates.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called the high number both a "moral failure" and an "economic catastrophe" .

This week, a major independent review , carried out by former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn, is expected to set out how the government should tackle the issue of Neets and make recommendations about getting more young people into work.

Some suggested changes to the welfare system have already been announced , but schools are expected to be asked to do more to make sure pupils are "work-ready" when they leave.

Any new recommendations will build on plans the government has already announced to allow students in England to choose new vocational GCSEs from age 14.

Ati is 14 and says she has been learning things about job interviews she did not know before.

"How to speak to people. How to present myself to different people," she says. "Like the fact you have to walk into a room and introduce yourself. I didn't think you really had to do that, but I think that's a good new skill that I've learned."

Fourteen-year-old Myla says Year 10 is "not too early" to be practising job interviews.

She says: "In two years we'll probably start looking at part-time jobs. It definitely helps with nerves and that kind of stuff if you've done it before and tried it before."

Careers teacher Paisley Charlton says the aim of these lessons is to make sure the students are ready for the working world. Since the school overhauled its careers education a couple of years ago, none of the students has become Neet on leaving at 18.

"We want to ensure they are confident within themselves to attend things like job interviews, to look for work experience and be able to talk about themselves in a positive way."

The school makes careers education a priority for students as soon as they join.

There is a "speed-networking" event in Year 7 where pupils have one-to-one chats with local employers. Posters describing nine "employability principles" - including resilience and problem-solving - are proudly displayed and followed in every lesson.

"We make sure careers isn't just something that happens at the end of school, or at transition points," says head teacher Ellen Walton. "It's a big world out there and we see it as a moral duty to make sure that we give them everything that they need to make the choices that are right for them.

"We work really hard to make sure they're all in education, employment or training when they leave us."

Around the country, other schools bring in outside organisations like Youth Careers Collective , a charity that works with dozens of schools in London.

Chief executive Matt Lent says they "act as a bridge between schools and businesses" by bringing employers into schools and disadvantaged pupils into the workplace for networking opportunities.

He says young people need opportunities to understand and develop employability skills, but "they aren't always embedded into the day-to-day school experience".

Lent warns that work to improve young people's "work-readiness" isn't enough to solve the Neets crisis, and he's "hopeful" that the imminent Milburn review will address this.

"Yes, we need to prepare young people for employment, but employers also need to take responsibility for creating accessible opportunities," he says.

How a borough in Merseyside is bucking the UK's youth unemployment trend

Teenagers to be offered new vocational GCSE subjects in school

Schools and colleges across England are legally required to have a careers programme, including expanded opportunities for work experience, and to use the updated Gatsby Benchmarks to structure their careers education.

The Gatsby Foundation's Beth Jones, who developed the guidance, says the more careers education benchmarks a school achieves, the less likely it is their students will leave as Neet.

"Careers guidance cannot solve every barrier young people face, but it is an important part of helping them navigate their futures successfully," she says.

There is no doubt that improving careers education and giving pupils more vocational options is part of the plan for schools, but it is not the whole picture for solving the Neet crisis.

As Milburn himself pointed out in his interim report earlier this year, from the moment a child arrives at school at age four, the system can predict "who is most likely to fail".

A child starting school without basic "school-ready" skills like potty training at ages four or five is nearly three times as likely to be Neet by the time they reach 16 or 17 years old.

Pupils with special educational needs, from poorer backgrounds, or those with mental health issues are also more likely to be Neet.

The problem might not be identifying the pupils that need help, but finding the funding to help them. The Institute for Fiscal Studies warned that a "one-size-fits-all approach" to the Neet crisis was "unlikely to work, given the very different circumstances of young people who are Neet".

It says a "key question for the government will be how much they are willing to invest in the short run in the hope of a pay-off in future years".

Back in the classroom, 15-year-old Riley is packing up at the end of her employability class.

She wants to go into acting or possibly work with animals, and thinks the skills she has learned will help her when it's time for her first job interview in the real world.

"You're able to learn a lot about yourself and how you can improve," Riley says.

"It's quite nice because it prepares me for the future."

articles.title: Hannah Fry feels 'unbelievably lucky' after cervical cancer treatment
articles.summary: The presenter says she has received a 'five-year clear' after having a hysterectomy in her thirties.
articles.body:
Prof Hannah Fry has described feeling "unbelievably lucky" after being treated for cervical cancer.

The mathematician and BBC presenter, who recently took part in the second season of the Celebrity Traitors, said cancerous cells were discovered after she attended a cervical screening in 2020.

She underwent a hysterectomy, describing the experience to BBC Radio 4's Desert Island Discs as "horrific".

"As awful as that was, it had a full stop at the end of the sentence," the 42-year-old added. "I had my five-year clear the other day. I feel so unbelievably lucky."

In Sunday's episode, Fry told show host Lauren Laverne that she had delayed a cervical screening examination for months in 2020. After she attended one, the results "didn't come back for a few weeks," she said.

"Then I got a call from my GP telling me they needed me to come back and do another test, and they did a biopsy.

"I was trying hard not to panic but when they found it was in the lymphatic system… that was when it really started to come down."

The broadcaster said she was told that her chances of survival depended on the cancerous cells not having spread to her lymph nodes, although it was not clear "how bad it was at that point".

"It's all about, basically, how far into your lymphatic system has it got. If it had not got into any lymph nodes, then the odds were in my favour and I had a really good chance of survival," she said.

Fry explained that this meant "if it was in one it would drop to a 60% chance of survival and two – the odds would go against me and it would be a 40% chance".

While in isolation in hospital following her hysterectomy, Fry said a surgeon told her that four of her lymph nodes had appeared enlarged.

She added: "I was in this hospital bed on my own and no-one could come and visit me for over a week, with nothing but the sheer terrifying drop of the end of my existence in front of me – it was horrific."

Fry described not being able to "think back to happy things that... have already happened because it is sad", while also not being able to "look forward to things you are hopeful about because it doesn't feel like it is there".

She also said she asked her then husband to set up FaceTime in the corner of a room so she could watch their two young daughters play while she was in hospital.

"I didn't want them to see me, it was too much," she said.

But she added: "Going through something like that I don't think I would swap it.

"I think it was honestly such a gift to have that experience when you're 36 and then come out the other side of it."

The presenter grew up in a working-class family and studied mathematics at University of College London.

She later completed a PhD in fluid dynamics, and last year became Cambridge University's first professor of the public understanding of mathematics.

Fry has fronted BBC science series including The Future with Hannah Fry and The Secret Genius of Modern Life.

She was banished in the latest series of The Celebrity Traitors after being exposed as a traitor.

articles.title: Carney says he’s ‘making progress’ with Trump on possible US-Canada trade deal
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Saturday trade negotiations between his government and the U.S. were progressing amid a monthslong tariff battle between the two countries. The leader told reporters in Manila he had a conversation with President Trump, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and other officials “just…
articles.body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Saturday trade negotiations between his government and the U.S. were progressing amid a monthslong tariff battle between the two countries.

The leader told reporters in Manila he had a conversation with President Trump, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and other officials “just before” heading to the Philippines for the Association of the Southeast Asian Nations’ (ASEAN) three-day summit, adding that Washington and Ottawa are “making progress.”

While the prime minister’s remarks suggest a renewed interest in resolving the U.S.-Canada trade war, he also stressed he would not “settle for a deal” that is inconsistent with “a viable Canadian auto sector.”

“This is one of the fundamental issues in our trade negotiation, and we are making progress,” Carney said.

In August, Canada walked away from trade negotiations with the U.S. after Carney said the Trump administration introduced eleventh-hour demands Ottawa was unwilling to meet.

The U.S. responded by imposing 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian exports. Canada reacted with retaliatory tariffs , with officials vowing to match Washington’s duties “dollar for dollar.”

In his Saturday remarks, the prime minister stressed the importance of the Canadian car manufacturing industry to the U.S., emphasizing the American auto sector depends partly on “the degree of integration” with its northern neighbor.

“This is one of the most challenging issues in the trade negotiations,” Carney said. “As I say, we’re making progress. We’re not there yet.”

Carney addressed Ottawa’s ongoing negotiations with Washington ahead of ASEAN’s three-day summit in Manila, at which Trump is also slated to appear. The prime minister’s press conference served to announce two Canadian deals with ASEAN and the Philippines, both of which aimed to reduce the North American country’s trading reliance on the U.S.

“Today’s announcements are part of a strategy of developing a dense web of reliable partners to create more opportunities for our businesses, more choice for Canadians, better jobs for our workers, and reducing our relative reliance on the United States,” Carney said.

The Canadian leader also told reporters his conversation with Trump ahead of his travels was “long” and “substantive.”

“There is a possibility of a deal, a bilateral deal, but we’re not yet there,” Carney said.

The prime minister said his government is “ahead of schedule” on its goals to double its non-U.S. exports in under a 10-year period. Almost one in three of Canada’s export dollars is currently coming from outside of the U.S., marking a 40-year high, according to Carney.

articles.title: Hundreds of men march in Switzerland to protest violence against women
articles.summary: Organisers say men must speak out, as Swiss study finds half of men aged 18 to 24 hold restrictive view of masculinity.
articles.body:
Hundreds of men have led a demonstration in Switzerland’s capital, Bern, to denounce misogyny and violence against women, saying men need to take a more effective role in fighting both.

The “Men Against Violence Against Women” rally outside parliament on Saturday follows persistent concerns that misogyny is too prevalent online among teenage boys and young men and that other men need to build a stronger counter-narrative.

The misogynistic views are pushed by the right-wing “manosphere” – a loose network of online forums and influencers that promote male supremacy and hostility to feminism. Such influencers were emboldened after Donald Trump won the US presidential election in 202 to justify and amplify misogynistic derision and threats online.

“We men are part of the problem – the problem being violence against women and queer people,” said Christoph Gosteli, a 42-year-old social worker who co-organised the rally with a group called maenner.

“That is why it is important for us to take a stand and say, ‘We no longer want to be part of the problem; we want to be part of the solution.’”

An academic and advocacy group survey released in June by the University of Zurich and MenCare, an umbrella group of Swiss men’s and fathers’ organisations, found that half of male respondents aged 18 to 24 held a “restrictive and dominance-based view of masculinity”, expressing concerns that “real men are increasingly marginalised in society”.

The study called for “a systematic and society-wide debate about ideals of masculinity that promote violence”, beginning in schools.

Swiss Justice Minister Beat Jans attended a conference earlier this month on the dangers of violent online abuse of women.

In a speech on November 2, he said that men commit four-fifths of violent crimes and that in rape cases, the share is “as high as 99 percent”.

“It is not all men. But we must also admit: It is almost always men,” Jans said. “Violence by men does not begin with the first blow; it begins with a disparaging remark. We men all have a duty.”

articles.body: A free baseball card handed out at a Seattle Mariners game has turned into an unexpectedly valuable collectible, earning a 13-year-old fan $20,100 at an online auction. Abby, a young baseball enthusiast from the Seattle area, had no idea that the card she received featured an extremely rare edition of a local internet sensation. According to reporting by The Seattle Times, republished by The Spokesman-Review, and additional coverage by People and MyNorthwest, the one-of-a-kind gold card featuring Jimothy, a viral Seattle raccoon, attracted 100 bids before selling on eBay on August 30, 2026. The unusual collectible was part of a special promotion organised by the Mariners at T-Mobile Park on August 5, when the team played the Detroit Tigers. The first 20,000 fans entering the stadium received a Jimothy-themed baseball trading card, turning the game into an opportunity for supporters to take home a piece of Seattle's latest internet craze. Among the thousands of cards distributed was a single gold edition, making it a one-of-one collectible. Abby happened to receive that particular card. She was initially unaware of just how unusual her find was. However, other fans quickly noticed its rarity and approached her during the game with offers to buy it. Her family decided against selling it immediately, choosing instead to understand its potential value.From a free giveaway to a five-figure auctionAbby's family eventually listed the card on eBay, where interest from collectors grew rapidly. The auction attracted approximately 100 bids and closed at $20,100 on Sunday evening, August 30. The sale also placed the Jimothy card among the most valuable stadium giveaway collectibles. According to The Athletic, its price surpassed the $19,800 fetched by a limited-edition Los Angeles Dodgers card featuring the popular Japanese manga and anime franchise One Piece, which had sold earlier in the year.Abby's mother, Jessie Nino, said the family wanted to make a sensible decision with the unexpected windfall. The proceeds are intended to support her daughter's future, including her college education and potentially a home purchase. The sale also highlights how sports memorabilia can acquire considerable value when an item combines limited availability with an unexpected cultural phenomenon.Who is Jimothy, the raccoon behind the collectible craze?Jimothy is not a baseball player or a team mascot in the traditional sense. The raccoon became an unlikely celebrity after videos and photographs of the animal roaming Seattle's Ballard neighbourhood began circulating online in July. What caught people's attention was his unusual appearance. Jimothy has a remarkably compact body and distinctive short spine, with his appearance believed to be associated with a rare condition called short spine syndrome.Videos of the animal attracted millions of views, turning him into a local favourite and eventually an internet sensation. The Mariners capitalised on the growing interest by organising dedicated Jimothy-themed events at the ballpark in August. Alongside the trading card giveaway, the team also offered special merchandise, including a themed T-shirt. A portion of the proceeds from a special ticket package was directed towards the Ballard Food Bank.For Abby, however, the biggest surprise came from a single card tucked into a giveaway sleeve. What began as a complimentary souvenir from a baseball game became a $20,100 collectible within weeks, demonstrating just how unpredictable the market for rare sports memorabilia can be.You use AI every day. articles.title: Private planes and roadtrips: AEW goes above and beyond to get to Phoenix for Full Gear despite travel chaos
articles.summary: Tony Khan dispatched private jets to hub locations to fly AEW talent to Phoenix after nationwide flight cancelations threatened Full Gear.
articles.body: All Elite Wrestling (AEW) dropkicked a nationwide nightmare to make sure its talent and personnel made it to Phoenix for Full Gear on Saturday despite travel chaos that plagued millions across the U.S. AEW owner Tony Khan brought in some wrestlers and other workers on private planes just to make sure they were going to show up for the fans, who were expected to pack the Mortgage Matchup Center for one of the company’s top pay-per-views on the calendar. "I know it’s been an incredibly challenging few days for a lot of people," Khan said in a video posted to his social media. "My sympathies to everybody affected by all of the flight cancelations and delays. Yesterday, as you can imagine, was a hectic day as it was for a lot of people with the flights grounded and that applied to all flights yesterday – private and public flights. For AEW, we’re the same as everyone else, we’re not trying to break any rules. Everybody was grounded and we started formulating a plan that has come together really, really well." CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE Khan said everyone on the Full Gear pay-per-view card arrived in Phoenix. Khan sent private planes at three "hub locations" to bring the wrestlers and other personnel to the Mortgage Matchup Center. The only thing that changed was the Tailgate Brawl – which will occur on the Full Gear pre-show. Khan said he believed everyone probably would have made it on their scheduled flights. "I think it was virtually impossible given how many flights of people who work in AEW have been canceled had I not dispatched the private planes to the three hub locations, I think it’s very unlikely everybody would have made it here. I think there probably would have been some changes to the main card." Adam Copeland, who battles Kazuchika Okada for the AEW International Championship, said it was "challenging" to get from the East Coast all the way to Phoenix. "I was going down the runway about to take off for Denver and the pilot came on and said there’s a ground stoppage nationwide. I was like, ‘OK.’ I called Beth (Phoenix) and she came and got me and I went home," he said. "No idea if I was going to make it today. All of my flights started getting canceled one after the other after the other. Everyone else’s flights were starting to take off but mine weren’t. "Even still, my flight to get out here is tomorrow at 5:37. So, Tony Khan sent a plane to come get us. Poor (Tony) Schiavone got there early so he was sitting there at 9 o’clock. I don’t think we were taking off until 11 so I was like, come have a coffee, come pet my dogs. We had a big dog cuddle-fest this morning and my girls got to meet Tony and we had some coffee – we made the best of it." Tony Schiavone, one-third of the AEW broadcast team, was set to fly out of Atlanta when he made the last-minute decision to take a smaller plane out of Asheville, North Carolina, because of the uncertainty that he may have been delayed or canceled. He told his wife he wasn’t going to drive all the way to Phoenix, but he would have if he had the time to make the 27-hour trip. "It was already a bad day to be a Buck but then I had to drive to Detroit, then drive to Chicago, then sit on a private jet, which is pretty awesome, but I had to sit on that jet for eight hours, waiting to get here to tear up these Young Bucks. "So, Tony Khan, thank you for that jet. Young Bucks, I don’t feel sorry for you." Matt and Nick Jackson – The Young Bucks – were only in California. They had to make the drive to Phoenix. "We told each other, we’re blessed, we’re in California. A lot of these guys are coming further than us, but we will do anything – planes, trains and automobiles – we will be here at Full Gear," Matt Jackson said. "We have a big match tonight – Davis and Doyle. Two intimidating meatheads that actually had our number the last couple times when we’ve been in the ring. We talked about it on the drive. Excalibur, Schiavone’s broadcast teammate, said he was at the gym when he got a text about the travel chaos. He said he planned to jump in a car to go from Southern California to Phoenix. He drove five hours to get to the arena but took solace in the fact he got a chance to stop in the desert he doesn’t normally stop in. "I made it. I wouldn’t miss this for the world. I know people have much tougher travel days than I did. I mean a five-hour drive, it’s doable, but in wrestling terms, it’s nothing," he said. "I wasn’t going to miss this for the world. I know a lot of people in AEW, everybody in AEW, has the same idea, same feeling, if there’s any way possible for them to be here today, they’re gonna be here at Full Gear. … There’s nothing that can keep me from Full Gear today." Nigel McGuinness, the third person on the broadcast team, got to Phoenix from Los Angeles. He jumped in his car when he learned about the travel woes. "There was no way I was gonna miss Full Gear," he said. "There’s something about being in professional wrestling where you make the show no matter what. I’ve never missed a show and there was no way I was going to miss Full Gear." articles.title: New Orleans port sues to get control of tanker that crashed into cruise ship on Mississippi River
articles.summary: Just hours after a tanker in New Orleans lost its steering and slammed into a docked river cruise boat, the city’s port sued to make sure federal investigators can seize the vessel that is owned by a subsidiary of a Chinese company.
articles.body: Just hours after a tanker in New Orleans lost its steering and slammed into a docked river cruise boat, the city’s port sued to make sure federal investigators can seize the vessel that is owned by a subsidiary of a Chinese company. All 197 passengers and crew on the American Heritage cruise ship survived Friday as well as the crew on the tanker. Officials said 32 people were brought to the hospital, including two police officers thrown into the Mississippi River when the boat rolled. But none of the injuries were critical and eight remained hospitalized Saturday. The National Transportation Safety Board said the tanker’s voyage data recorder has been recovered. The device records information such as the vessel’s speed and audio from the bridge of the tanker. It is the maritime equivalent of an aircraft’s flight data recorder. NTSB member John DeLeeuw said the agency expects to release a preliminary report within 30 days, with the final investigation report expected in 18 to 24 months. A 16-member team will spend a week in New Orleans investigating the incident. Lawsuit leads to warrant to get control of tanker The lawsuit, filed by the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans, said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker caused at least $1 million in damage to its terminal. A judge issued a warrant Friday giving federal officials control of the ship for now. The tanker has been towed away from the site, but it could take weeks to move the cruise ship, which remains turned on its side against a terminal in the Mississippi River, Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham told reporters Saturday. The first step is to make sure the 16,000 gallons (60,500 liters) of fuel on the boat are removed safely, she said. Traffic has been limited on the Mississippi River, but Burnham said boats should be able to move both upstream and downstream soon. The tanker appeared to lose steering, but the exact cause of the crash is not known, Burnham said. The National Transportation Safety Board was sending investigators to New Orleans. Survivor recalls harrowing minutes in the river The first warning people on board the American Heritage had was the tanker blasting its horn several times as it floated toward the cruise ship, passenger Joe Knab told WDSU-TV. The hit was hard, and the ship immediately started leaning. The crew gathered everyone on the third deck to put on life vests and start getting them off the boat, but it suddenly rolled and sent Knab and about 100 other passengers and crew into the muddy Mississippi River, where the water was 66 degrees Fahrenheit (19 degrees Celsius). Tugboat operators, other cruise ship captains, nearby workers, police and other rescuers rushed to help. “It’s fine now, but it was a little scary there at the time. I thought I was drowning because I kept bobbing underneath — and the water doesn’t taste very good,” Knab told the television station, still in the jeans he was wearing on the boat, now covered in mud. Knab said he thinks he was in the water about 15 minutes. He laughed and said his 20 years in the Navy likely helped him. “They taught us not to drown,” Knab said. Knab was wearing a shirt from a Hilton hotel where the passengers gathered. The rest of his belongings were in the river. Somehow his cellphone still worked. He hoped to get on a plane soon back to Wichita, Kansas, but he was not sure how Friday’s nationwide ground stop was going to throw another problem at him. Putting the life vests on the passengers as they waited to get off the boat likely saved a number of lives when the boat suddenly turned into the water, New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said. “Whether it’s 10 feet of water or 200 feet, having those vests, having that population put those vests on and kind of float upriver while we retrieve them — I think was the best factor of success,” Montroll said. The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations. Tanker owner is subsidiary of Chinese company The Atlantic Asphalt is a 520-foot-long (160-meter-long) vessel. It had a final destination in New Orleans, according to MarineTraffic, and was sailing under a flag for the Marshall Islands. The ship is owned by a company called Nave Shipping SA, which is registered in Monrovia, Liberia, according to the International Maritime Organization and was one of the defendants in the lawsuit filed Friday. Nave Shipping is a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a sprawling Chinese state-owned conglomerate, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic. China State Shipbuilding Corp. didn’t respond to an emailed request for comment. The tanker involved in the crash specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to MarineTraffic.

articles.title: Israeli air strike kills senior Hamas commander in Gaza
articles.summary: Hamas confirms the death of Rafah brigade commander Samir Abu Younis in an attack on Khan Younis on Saturday.
articles.body:
Hamas has confirmed that Rafah brigade commander Samir Abu Younis was killed in an Israeli air strike on the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis, southern Gaza.

Israel’s military and Shin Bet security agency earlier said in a joint statement that they had targeted a senior Hamas military commander in a drone strike in Khan Younis on Saturday.

The attack that hit a tent sheltering displaced people wounded two others.

The casualties were taken to Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, medical personnel told Al Jazeera on Saturday.

Video footage verified by Al Jazeera and posted by Palestinian journalists from the vicinity of the hospital showed ambulances inside the grounds and stretchers that appear to be stained with blood.

Al-Mawasi, a coastal strip on the Mediterranean, is crowded with displaced Palestinians living in tents. Israel has repeatedly attacked the area despite previously designating it a humanitarian zone.

Gaza’s Ministry of Health said in its latest update on Saturday that Israeli attacks have killed 16 people and injured 68 others over the past 48 hours.

Since the “ceasefire” in Gaza took effect on October 11, 2025, Israel has killed at least 1,643 Palestinians and injured 5,964. At least 850 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

Since Israel began its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, at least 74,695 people have been killed and 176,093 injured, according to the Health Ministry.

The ministry also reported that the number of deaths related to cold has risen to 11 after a nine-month-old baby died from hypothermia, the first this winter.

Gaza’s residents, most of whom have been displaced, are living in tents and damaged buildings as water damage from recent heavy rains has set in.

Israeli attacks have escalated across Gaza, despite the October ceasefire.
