articles.title: A Cambridge dealer bought a forgotten painting for £150 at auction after spotting Dalí's signature, only to discover it was worth £45,700
articles.summary: A Salvador Dalí artwork discovered in a London garage has sold for £45,700 after a Cambridge antiques dealer purchased it for just £150 at a house
articles.body: A Salvador Dalí artwork discovered in a London garage has sold for £45,700 after a Cambridge antiques dealer purchased it for just £150 at a house clearance auction. The unusual 1966 illustration, titled Vecchio Sultano, depicts a bejewelled old sultan and was initially overlooked by bidders despite carrying the artist's signature. Its authenticity was later confirmed by renowned Dalí expert Nicolas Descharnes after examining its style, colours and paper. The artwork was part of Dalí's unfinished The Arabian Nights project, for which he completed just 100 of the planned 500 illustrations before abandoning the collection.Salvador Dalí's signed 1966 illustration goes unnoticed at auctionThe unusual illustration was reportedly discovered in the garage of a London home before being put up for sale at a house clearance auction in Cambridge. Despite carrying Dalí's signature in the bottom-right corner, the artwork did not attract significant attention when it appeared at the auction. According to The Guardian, the sale attracted just two bidders, with the winning offer coming from Cambridge-based antiques dealer John Russell, whose name was changed in the report.Russell purchased the artwork for £150 after spotting the artist's signature. Recalling his experience, he told The Guardian: “Most of the time, I buy stuff that I like.” He also explained that he was taking a chance on the purchase because he was not certain he would want to display the unusual illustration himself. The painting was subsequently identified as a 1966 work depicting an old sultan.A Sotheby's catalogue helps trace the history of the £150 Salvador Dalí paintingAfter purchasing the illustration, Russell noticed stickers on its reverse side indicating that it had previously been listed in a Sotheby's auction catalogue during the 1990s. This prompted him to investigate its history further. A few months after the purchase, he located the relevant Sotheby's sale catalogue through eBay in the United States. The catalogue listed the artwork, measuring 38cm by 29cm, and showed that it had previously been identified as Dalí's work.Russell then approached Cheffins, an auction house based in Cambridge, to obtain a professional valuation. According to the report, he had decided to bid for the artwork on the spur of the moment, relying partly on his experience of watching the BBC television programme Fake or Fortune. The discovery of the Sotheby's catalogue provided an important reference point for further examination and authentication of the illustration.Nicolas Descharnes confirms the authenticity of the Dalí illustrationCheffins consulted Nicolas Descharnes, a recognised expert on Salvador Dalí, to establish whether the artwork was genuine. After examining the illustration, Descharnes certified it as authentic. His assessment considered the style, subject matter and colours of the picture, alongside the quality and dimensions of the paper, which he said were consistent with other illustrations from the same series.The artwork was created using mixed media, including watercolour paint and felt-tip. It depicts a bejewelled sultan and differs in style from many of Dalí's better-known surrealist paintings. Explaining the distinction in his interview with The Guardian, Descharnes said: “People expect to see very surrealist pieces by Dalí. This one is not surrealist, but it’s a Dalí.” Fine art specialist Gabrielle Downie of Cheffins also discussed the artist's interest in Moorish culture, explaining that it influenced the subject matter of the illustration.Vecchio Sultano joins the history of Dalí's abandoned Arabian Nights projectVecchio Sultano belongs to a larger collection of illustrations commissioned by Dalí's patrons, Giuseppe and Mara Albaretto. The project was intended to include 500 illustrations inspired by The Arabian Nights, a collection of Middle Eastern folktales. However, Dalí abandoned the project after completing just 100 illustrations, leaving the intended collection unfinished.According to Downie, around half of the completed illustrations remained with Italian publishing house Rizzoli, where some were either damaged or lost. The remaining 50 stayed with the Albaretto family and were later inherited by their daughter, Christina, who was also Dalí's goddaughter. These 50 illustrations were eventually published in 2014, bringing renewed attention to the unfinished project and the whereabouts of the other works. articles.title: Fifth Canadian soldier dies of injuries from military training fire
articles.summary: A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries suffered when a wind-driven grass fire swept through troops during a military training exercise last month, the Canadian Armed Forces said Saturday.
articles.body: EDMONTON, Alberta — A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries suffered when a wind-driven grass fire swept through troops during a military training exercise last month, the Canadian Armed Forces said Saturday. Pvt. William Douglas Dal Bianco died Friday at a hospital in Ontario, where he had been receiving treatment since the Oct. 17 fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, the military said. About 84 soldiers from the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, were conducting attack training when winds pushed flames from a grass fire toward the troops at the base southeast of Edmonton. The military said Saturday that 24 soldiers remain hospitalized. “Private Dal Bianco and his fellow soldiers were training to defend Canada,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a social media post. “With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours. That is service.” The other soldiers killed were Pvt. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Saskatchewan; Pvt. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, British Columbia; Pvt. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, British Columbia; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton. Military police are investigating the fire, while a separate military board of inquiry will examine the circumstances of the tragedy and recommend measures to prevent similar incidents. Carney has called the fire one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military on Canadian soil.

articles.title: Iraq PM sacks nine officials over oil smuggling in pro-Iran stronghold
articles.summary: Dismissals follow probe that uncovered illegal oil refineries and smuggling in a region run by Kataib Hezbollah.
articles.body:
Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has dismissed nine senior security officials over an alleged oil smuggling operation in the Jurf al-Nasr area, a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group.

Al-Zaidi chaired an emergency security meeting to review the findings of a committee investigating smuggling in Jurf al-Nasr, Babil province, military spokesperson Sabah al-Numan told the Iraqi News Agency (INA).

The move follows an investigation that uncovered illegal oil refineries and evidence of manipulation linked to the smuggling activities.

“In light of the investigation’s findings, [the prime minister] ordered that all individuals accused of involvement in oil smuggling operations be referred to the judiciary,” al-Numan said.

The prime minister “also ordered the dismissal” of nine officials, including security and intelligence officers in Babil province, an Interior Ministry commander, and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil, he said.

The police chief of Babil province was among those dismissed.

Kataib Hezbollah, an Iran-aligned paramilitary group and one of Iraq’s most heavily armed factions, has recently issued several sharp statements against the prime minister, threatening his government and accusing him of corruption.

Senior Iraqi politicians previously told the AFP news agency that al-Zaidi had repeatedly said he was ready to confront groups refusing to disarm.

Al Jazeera’s Peter Smith, reporting from Baghdad, said previous Iraqi governments had been careful not to address the issue of an alleged oil smuggling network worth up to $30m monthly.

“This area had effectively been run as a state within a state until now,” Smith said. “But that seems to have changed, with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi saying that no inch of Iraq will be allowed to have oil smuggling operations like this.”

Two strategic oil pipelines running through the south of the country, just south of Baghdad, “had effectively been tapped into”, Smith said, citing a leaked intelligence report. “Oil was being siphoned off, stolen, and then sold on the black market in an operation worth tens of millions of dollars every month.”

On Wednesday, the INA reported that “intelligence documents” containing satellite images “showed crude oil and oil-derivatives smuggling operations carried out by an armed faction” in Jurf al-Nasr, accusing an unnamed group of tapping into a pipeline there.

Al-Numan said the investigating committee “confirmed the accuracy” of the information.

Akeel Abbas, a senior non-resident fellow at the Iraq Initiative within the Atlantic Council, told Al Jazeera that oil smuggling by various political factions and armed groups “is common in Iraq” due to “commercial rather than political or strategic” gains.

Abbas said the latest crackdown has more to do with “militia disarmament”.

“The prime minister cleverly decided to frame it as anticorruption. That is why a few days ago, there was a report leaked by the government about this operation,” he said.

The prime minister wants to “cut off the financial lifeline to this particular group that has been so resistant” to the government’s “militia disarmament” initiatives, he added.
